observations.seen: Frame 2 (autumn course) is lit almost flat, with little key/fill separation on the golfers. Frame 3 (cinder course) has a muddy brown cast that flattens the tee and fairway into one value range. Frame 1's overcast light reads best.

The night frame shows a crisp directional shadow from the golfer, and frame 1 has tree shadows on the fairway. In frames 2 and 3 the player contact shadows are faint soft blobs, and the trees cast no readable shadow.
No environment reflections are visible. The club shaft and the ball have only a weak specular highlight, and the cart and tee markers show no sky response.

The fairways are flat, empty planes running to a hard horizon line. No flag, green, hazard, or terrain undulation is visible in frames 2-4. Set dressing is limited to repeated blob trees and small cone shrubs. The cinder course is a flat hex-tile plane.

There is mild distance haze near the horizon in frames 1 and 3, and floating particles (embers, motes, stars) in all frames. The particles read as uniform noise and do not sit in the depth of the scene.

The grass has a fine noise texture that tiles visibly on the fairway. The tee box is a plain rectangle with a dark border slab. The tee markers are untextured red boxes, and the clothing is flat diffuse.

The golfer and caddie are low-poly with stiff, mannequin-like poses. The trees are stacked spheres on cylinders, and the shrubs are cones. The golf cart in frame 1 is the most detailed asset in the set.

In frames 2-4 the golfer is pushed to the far left edge, and the caddie is cut off by the frame. The centre and right of the frame are mostly empty fairway, with only the white aim line leading the eye.

The camera is a low third-person view from behind and to the right, not the elevated broadcast angle the recipe calls for. The subject fills roughly 15-25% of the frame, and the horizon sits dead centre, which emphasises the emptiness.
The aim line blooms lightly in the night frame. Tone mapping is acceptable, but the cinder frame is low-contrast and murky. No colour grading gives the courses a consistent identity.
